brihadaranyaka-4-5-12.translation: As the ocean is the meeting place of all waters, so the skin is of all touches, the nose of all smells, the tongue of all tastes, the eye of all forms, the ear of all sounds, the mind of all intentions, the heart of all knowledge, the hands of all work, the sexual organ of all pleasures, the anus of all excretions, the feet of all journeys, and speech of all Vedas.
brihadaranyaka-4-5-12.meaning: Each kind of experience has its gathering point, as all waters gather in the sea.
brihadaranyaka-4-5-12.explanation: Ultimately, all of these meet in the Self, just as every river ends in the ocean.

brihadaranyaka-4-5-13.translation: As a lump of salt has no inside or outside but is wholly taste, so this Self has no inside or outside but is wholly a mass of awareness. Arising from these elements, it vanishes again into them. After death there is no separate awareness, I tell you. So said Yajnavalkya.
brihadaranyaka-4-5-13.meaning: The Self is pure awareness through and through; after death, separate identity ends.
brihadaranyaka-4-5-13.explanation: Like salt that is salty all the way through, the Self is awareness all the way through. When the body ends, the sense of being a separate individual dissolves.

brihadaranyaka-4-5-14.translation: Maitreyi said: 'Here, sir, you have confused me. I do not understand this.' He said: 'I am not saying anything confusing. This Self is imperishable; its nature is never to be cut off.'
brihadaranyaka-4-5-14.meaning: Yajnavalkya reassures her: the Self never perishes.
brihadaranyaka-4-5-14.explanation: Maitreyi worries that 'no awareness after death' means annihilation. He clarifies that the Self itself is indestructible; only the sense of separateness ends.

brihadaranyaka-4-5-15.translation: Where there is a seeming duality, one sees, smells, tastes, speaks to, hears, thinks of, touches and knows another. But where everything has become one's own Self, by what and whom should one see, smell, taste, speak to, hear, think of, touch or know? How can one know that by which all this is known? This Self is 'not this, not this'. It cannot be grasped, it does not decay, it does not cling, it is unbound, it does not suffer or come to harm. How can one know the knower? You have been taught, Maitreyi. This much, truly, is immortality. Saying this, Yajnavalkya went away.
brihadaranyaka-4-5-15.meaning: When all is the Self, there is no 'other' to perceive; the knower itself cannot be made an object.
brihadaranyaka-4-5-15.explanation: The dialogue ends with the 'neti neti' teaching. The Self is the subject of all knowing, so it can never be seen like an object. Having shared this, Yajnavalkya leaves for the life of a renunciant.

brihadaranyaka-4-6-1.translation: Now the line of teachers: Pautimashya from Gaupavana, Gaupavana from Pautimashya, Pautimashya from Gaupavana, Gaupavana from Kaushika, Kaushika from Kaundinya, Kaundinya from Shandilya, Shandilya from Kaushika and Gautama, Gautama...
brihadaranyaka-4-6-1.meaning: The lineage of teachers who passed down this teaching begins.
brihadaranyaka-4-6-1.explanation: Like 2.6, this list records who received the teaching from whom, honouring the chain of transmission. It continues in the next verses.

brihadaranyaka-4-6-2.translation: ...from Agniveshya, Agniveshya from Gargya, Gargya from Gargya, Gargya from Gautama, Gautama from Saitava, Saitava from Parasharyayana, and so on through Uddalakayana, Jabalayana, Madhyandinayana, Saukarayana, Kashayana, Sayakayana and Kaushikayani...
brihadaranyaka-4-6-2.meaning: The line of teachers continues back through many names.
brihadaranyaka-4-6-2.explanation: Each name is a teacher who learned from the one named after. The list shows the teaching was carefully handed down.

brihadaranyaka-4-6-3.translation: ...from Ghritakaushika, through Parasharya, Jatukarnya, Asurayana and Yaska, Traivani, Aupajandhani, Asuri, Bharadvaja, Atreya, Manti, Gautama, Vatsya, Shandilya, Kaishorya Kapya, Kumaraharita, Galava, Vidarbhi-kaundinya, Vatsanapat Babhrava, Pathas Saubhara, Ayasya Angirasa, Abhuti Tvashtra, Vishvarupa Tvashtra, the Ashvins, Dadhyanch Atharvana, Atharvan Daiva, Mrityu Pradhvamsana, Pradhvamsana, Ekarshi, Viprajitti, Vyashti, Sanaru, Sanatana, Sanaga, Parameshthin, and Brahman. Brahman is self-existent. Homage to Brahman.
brihadaranyaka-4-6-3.meaning: The lineage reaches back to the gods and finally to Brahman, the self-existent source.
brihadaranyaka-4-6-3.explanation: The chain moves from human teachers to divine ones and ends at Brahman itself, showing that the teaching's ultimate source is reality itself. It closes with a salutation.

brihadaranyaka-5-1-1.translation: That is full; this is full. From the full, the full arises. Taking the full from the full, the full alone remains. Brahman is space; the ancient one is space; space is the airy one, said the son of Kauravyayani. This is the Veda, the priests know; by it one knows what is to be known.
brihadaranyaka-5-1-1.meaning: The infinite whole stays whole no matter what comes from it.
brihadaranyaka-5-1-1.explanation: This famous verse, used as a peace chant, says the unseen reality (that) and the visible world (this) are both complete. Nothing taken from infinity reduces it. Brahman is then compared to space, which holds everything.

brihadaranyaka-5-2-1.translation: The three kinds of children of Prajapati, gods, humans and demons, lived as students with their father Prajapati. After their studies, the gods said: 'Teach us, sir.' He spoke the syllable 'Da' and asked, 'Did you understand?' They said, 'We understood. You told us: Damyata, be self-controlled.' 'Yes,' he said, 'you have understood.'
brihadaranyaka-5-2-1.meaning: For the gods, 'Da' means: control yourselves.
brihadaranyaka-5-2-1.explanation: The famous 'Da Da Da' teaching. The creator gives one syllable, and each group hears the lesson it most needs. The gods, given to pleasure, need self-restraint.

brihadaranyaka-5-2-2.translation: Then the humans said to him: 'Teach us, sir.' He spoke the same syllable 'Da' and asked, 'Did you understand?' They said, 'We understood. You told us: Datta, give.' 'Yes,' he said, 'you have understood.'
brihadaranyaka-5-2-2.explanation: Humans tend to hold on to what they have, so the lesson they hear in the same syllable is generosity.

brihadaranyaka-5-2-3.translation: Then the demons said to him: 'Teach us, sir.' He spoke the same syllable 'Da' and asked, 'Did you understand?' They said, 'We understood. You told us: Dayadhvam, be compassionate.' 'Yes,' he said, 'you have understood.' The divine voice of thunder repeats this: 'Da, Da, Da': be self-controlled, give, be compassionate. One should learn these three: self-control, giving and compassion.
brihadaranyaka-5-2-3.meaning: Thunder still teaches all of us three things: self-control, generosity and compassion.
brihadaranyaka-5-2-3.explanation: The demons, given to cruelty, hear compassion. The verse ends by saying every thunderclap repeats this lesson. Many read all three as meant for every person, since each of us has godlike, human and demonic tendencies.

brihadaranyaka-5-3-1.translation: The heart is Prajapati; it is Brahman; it is all this. 'Hridayam' has three syllables. 'Hri': his own people and others bring him offerings, one who knows this. 'Da': his own people and others give to him. 'Yam': he goes to the heavenly world, one who knows this.
brihadaranyaka-5-3-1.meaning: The heart is the centre of everything; each syllable of its name carries a blessing.
brihadaranyaka-5-3-1.explanation: The word for heart, hṛdayam, is broken into three syllables, linked to bringing (hṛ), giving (da) and going (i/yam). It is a playful way of saying the heart holds the whole of life.

brihadaranyaka-5-4-1.translation: That was indeed this, and it was simply the truth. Whoever knows this great, first-born wonder as 'Brahman is truth' conquers these worlds. How could one who knows this great, first-born wonder as 'Brahman is truth' be conquered? For Brahman is truth.
brihadaranyaka-5-4-1.meaning: Know that ultimate reality is truth, and you cannot be defeated.
brihadaranyaka-5-4-1.explanation: Truth (satya) is presented as the first thing to arise and as Brahman itself. Holding to truth makes one invincible.

brihadaranyaka-5-5-1.translation: In the beginning this world was just water. The water produced truth; truth is Brahman. Brahman produced Prajapati, and Prajapati the gods. The gods worship truth alone. 'Satyam' has three syllables: 'sa', 'ti', 'yam'. The first and last syllables are truth; the middle is untruth. Untruth is held on both sides by truth, so truth prevails. Untruth does not harm one who knows this.
brihadaranyaka-5-5-1.meaning: Truth surrounds and overpowers untruth; the one who knows this cannot be hurt by lies.
brihadaranyaka-5-5-1.explanation: A syllable play: the outer parts of the word 'satyam' are said to be truth and the middle one untruth. Since truth hems in falsehood on both sides, truth always wins.

brihadaranyaka-5-5-2.translation: That truth is the sun. The person in the sun's disc and the person in the right eye rest on each other: the one in the sun rests on this one through its rays, and this one rests on that through the breaths. When a person is about to die, they see the disc as plain; the rays no longer come back to them.
brihadaranyaka-5-5-2.meaning: The person in the sun and the person in the eye are linked; at death the link fades.
brihadaranyaka-5-5-2.explanation: Old Indian thought linked the light of the eye with the light of the sun. The verse says they support each other, and at the time of death the eye no longer receives the sun's rays.

brihadaranyaka-5-5-3.translation: Of the person in the sun's disc, 'bhūḥ' is the head: one head, one syllable. 'Bhuvaḥ' is the arms: two arms, two syllables. 'Svaḥ' is the feet: two feet, two syllables. Its secret name is 'day' (ahar). One who knows this destroys and leaves behind evil.
brihadaranyaka-5-5-3.meaning: The three sacred words form the body of the person in the sun; its secret name is 'day'.
brihadaranyaka-5-5-3.explanation: The three great utterances (bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ) are matched by syllable count to head, arms and feet. 'Ahar' is linked to the verb 'to destroy' (han), so knowing it removes evil.

brihadaranyaka-5-5-4.translation: Of the person in the right eye, 'bhūḥ' is the head: one head, one syllable. 'Bhuvaḥ' is the arms: two arms, two syllables. 'Svaḥ' is the feet: two feet, two syllables. Its secret name is 'I' (aham). One who knows this destroys and leaves behind evil.
brihadaranyaka-5-5-4.meaning: The person in the eye has the same body; its secret name is 'I'.
brihadaranyaka-5-5-4.explanation: The same pattern applied inside us. The inner person's secret name is 'aham', meaning 'I', again linked to destroying evil.

brihadaranyaka-5-6-1.translation: This person, made of mind, whose nature is light, is inside the heart like a grain of rice or barley. It is the lord of all, the ruler of all, and governs everything that exists.
brihadaranyaka-5-6-1.meaning: A tiny light within the heart rules the whole universe.
brihadaranyaka-5-6-1.explanation: The inner person is described as very small and very great at once: as small as a grain, yet the ruler of everything.

brihadaranyaka-5-7-1.translation: They say lightning is Brahman. It is called lightning (vidyut) because it cuts (vidāna). One who knows lightning as Brahman cuts away their evil. For lightning is Brahman.
brihadaranyaka-5-7-1.meaning: Meditate on lightning as Brahman, and your faults are cut away.
brihadaranyaka-5-7-1.explanation: A word play links vidyut, lightning, with the idea of cutting or splitting. Like lightning splitting darkness, this knowledge splits off wrongdoing.

brihadaranyaka-5-8-1.translation: One should meditate on speech as a cow. It has four teats: the calls 'svāhā', 'vaṣaṭ', 'hanta' and 'svadhā'. The gods live on two of them, svāhā and vaṣaṭ; humans on hanta; the ancestors on svadhā. Breath is its bull, and mind its calf.
brihadaranyaka-5-8-1.meaning: Speech nourishes gods, people and ancestors like a cow feeding everyone.
brihadaranyaka-5-8-1.explanation: Each ritual call feeds a different group: offerings to gods, hospitality to people ('hanta', here, take this), offerings to ancestors. Breath gives speech power and mind follows it like a calf.

brihadaranyaka-5-9-1.translation: The universal fire within a person is what digests the food that is eaten. Its sound is what one hears when covering the ears. When one is about to die, one no longer hears that sound.
brihadaranyaka-5-9-1.meaning: The inner fire of digestion is the universal fire; its hum fades at death.
brihadaranyaka-5-9-1.explanation: Cover your ears and you hear a low roar. The text calls it the sound of the digestive fire, Vaishvanara. Its silence is a sign that life is leaving.

brihadaranyaka-5-10-1.translation: When a person leaves this world, they come to the wind. The wind opens for them a hole like the hole of a chariot wheel, and through it they rise up. They come to the sun, which opens for them a hole like that of a drum frame, and they rise further. They come to the moon, which opens a hole like that of a kettledrum, and they rise further. They come to a world without sorrow and without cold, and live there for endless years.
brihadaranyaka-5-10-1.meaning: After death the knower rises through wind, sun and moon to a world free of sorrow.
brihadaranyaka-5-10-1.explanation: A picture of the soul's upward journey. Each realm opens a gap for the departing person until they reach a lasting world without grief.

brihadaranyaka-5-11-1.translation: This is the highest austerity: that a sick person suffers. One who knows this wins the highest world. This is the highest austerity: that the dead are carried to the forest. One who knows this wins the highest world. This is the highest austerity: that the dead are placed on the fire. One who knows this wins the highest world.
brihadaranyaka-5-11-1.meaning: Illness, death and cremation can be seen as the highest spiritual discipline.
brihadaranyaka-5-11-1.explanation: The verse reframes suffering. If one sees sickness and the end of life as austerity, as a spiritual practice, then even these become a path to the highest state.

brihadaranyaka-5-12-1.translation: Some say food is Brahman. That is not so, for food rots without breath. Some say breath is Brahman. That is not so, for breath dries up without food. Only when these two deities become one do they reach the highest state. Pratrida asked his father: 'What good could I do to one who knows this, or what harm?' His father waved his hand: 'Don't, Pratrida. Who reaches the highest by merging these two?' And he told him: 'Vi': food is 'vi', for all beings enter (viś) food. 'Ram': breath is 'ram', for all beings delight (ram) in breath. All beings enter into, and delight in, one who knows this.
brihadaranyaka-5-12-1.meaning: Food and breath need each other; neither alone is the highest.
brihadaranyaka-5-12-1.explanation: Neither food nor breath is the ultimate on its own. The father hints that the knower has gone beyond being helped or harmed, and then gives the meditation 'vi-ram' linking food and breath.

brihadaranyaka-5-13-1.translation: The Uktha: breath is the Uktha, for breath raises up (utthāpayati) all this. A hero who knows the Uktha rises from him. One who knows this wins union with and the world of the Uktha.
brihadaranyaka-5-13-1.meaning: Breath is the hymn that lifts everything up.
brihadaranyaka-5-13-1.explanation: The Uktha is a recited hymn. Its name is linked to 'raising up', which is what breath does for the body.

brihadaranyaka-5-13-2.translation: The Yajus: breath is the Yajus, for all beings are joined (yujyante) in breath. All beings join with him for his excellence. One who knows this wins union with and the world of the Yajus.
brihadaranyaka-5-13-2.meaning: Breath is the sacrificial formula that joins all beings together.
brihadaranyaka-5-13-2.explanation: Yajus, the sacrificial formulas, is linked by sound to 'yuj', to join. Breath is what holds all living things together.

brihadaranyaka-5-13-3.translation: The Saman: breath is the Saman, for all beings come together (samyañci) in breath. All beings come together for his excellence. One who knows this wins union with and the world of the Saman.
brihadaranyaka-5-13-3.meaning: Breath is the chant that unites all beings.
brihadaranyaka-5-13-3.explanation: Saman, the sung chant, is linked to 'sam', together. Breath brings all beings into harmony.

brihadaranyaka-5-13-4.translation: The Kshatra: breath is the Kshatra, for breath protects (trāyate) the body from wounds (kṣaṇitoḥ). One who knows this reaches a protecting power that needs no other protection, and wins union with and the world of the Kshatra.
brihadaranyaka-5-13-4.meaning: Breath is the protecting power that guards the body.
brihadaranyaka-5-13-4.explanation: Kshatra, ruling power, is explained as 'protecting from harm'. Breath is the body's natural guardian.

brihadaranyaka-5-14-1.translation: Earth, mid-space, sky: these make eight syllables. One foot of the Gayatri has eight syllables. So this is its first foot. One who knows this foot of it wins as much as there is in the three worlds.
brihadaranyaka-5-14-1.meaning: The first foot of the Gayatri is the three worlds.
brihadaranyaka-5-14-1.explanation: The Gayatri metre has three feet of eight syllables. In Sanskrit, bhūmi, antarikṣa, dyauḥ total eight syllables, so they make up its first foot.

brihadaranyaka-5-14-2.translation: The Rig, Yajur and Sama verses: these make eight syllables. One foot of the Gayatri has eight syllables. So this is its second foot. One who knows this foot of it wins as much as the threefold knowledge covers.
brihadaranyaka-5-14-2.meaning: The second foot of the Gayatri is the three Vedas.
brihadaranyaka-5-14-2.explanation: The names of the three Vedas also add up to eight syllables, so they form the second foot. Knowing this brings all that the Vedas contain.

brihadaranyaka-5-14-3.translation: In-breath, out-breath, diffused breath: these make eight syllables. One foot of the Gayatri has eight syllables. So this is its third foot. One who knows this foot of it wins as much as there are living beings. Its fourth, visible foot, beyond the dust, is the one who shines yonder (the sun). 'Fourth' is turīya. 'Visible foot' because it is seen. 'Beyond the dust' because it shines above all the dust. One who knows this foot of it shines with glory and fame.
brihadaranyaka-5-14-3.meaning: The third foot is breath; the hidden fourth foot is the shining sun beyond all.
brihadaranyaka-5-14-3.explanation: The three breaths make the third foot. Then a fourth foot is named: the sun, shining above the 'dust' of the world. This fourth, beyond the three, points to the highest.

brihadaranyaka-5-14-4.translation: This Gayatri rests on that fourth, visible foot beyond the dust. That rests on truth. The eye is truth. So if two people come arguing, one saying 'I saw it', the other 'I heard it', we would believe the one who says 'I saw it'. Truth rests on strength. Breath is strength. So people say strength is mightier than truth. Thus the Gayatri rests on what is within the self. It protected the gayas: the gayas are the breaths. Because it protected (tatre) the gayas, it is called Gayatri. The Savitri verse one recites is this very one. It protects the breaths of the one to whom it is recited.
brihadaranyaka-5-14-4.meaning: The Gayatri protects life-breath, which is why it is called Gayatri.
brihadaranyaka-5-14-4.explanation: A chain of support: Gayatri rests on the sun, which rests on truth (the eye), which rests on strength (breath). The name is explained as 'protector of the breaths'. The Savitri mantra taught to students is this Gayatri.

brihadaranyaka-5-14-5.translation: Some teach the Savitri in the Anushtubh metre, saying, 'Speech is Anushtubh; we teach speech.' One should not do that. One should teach the Savitri in the Gayatri metre. Even if one who knows this accepts a great deal in gifts, it is not equal to a single foot of the Gayatri.
brihadaranyaka-5-14-5.meaning: Teach the Savitri in the Gayatri metre; no gift equals even one foot of it.
brihadaranyaka-5-14-5.explanation: A ruling on how to teach the mantra, followed by praise: knowing the Gayatri so outweighs gifts that accepting them does the knower no harm.

brihadaranyaka-5-14-6.translation: If one accepted these three worlds full of wealth, that would equal the first foot of the Gayatri. If one accepted as much as the threefold knowledge covers, that would equal the second foot. If one accepted as much as there are living beings, that would equal the third foot. Its fourth, visible foot beyond the dust, the one who shines yonder, cannot be reached by anything. How could one accept so much?
brihadaranyaka-5-14-6.meaning: Even all the worlds as a gift would equal only one foot of the Gayatri.
brihadaranyaka-5-14-6.explanation: The worth of the Gayatri is beyond measure. Its fourth foot, the highest, cannot be matched by any gift at all.

brihadaranyaka-5-14-7.translation: Its worship: 'O Gayatri, you are one-footed, two-footed, three-footed, four-footed. You are footless, for you are not walked on. Homage to your fourth, visible foot beyond the dust!' If one hates someone: 'May that person not gain that', or 'May that wish of his not succeed.' The wish of one against whom this is used does not succeed. Or one may say, 'May I gain that.'
brihadaranyaka-5-14-7.meaning: A prayer to the Gayatri as having all feet and yet none.
brihadaranyaka-5-14-7.explanation: The Gayatri is honoured as both having parts and being beyond all parts. The text then notes the old belief that this worship could be used to block an enemy's wish or to gain one's own.

brihadaranyaka-5-14-8.translation: Janaka of Videha said to Budila Ashvatarashvi: 'You called yourself a knower of the Gayatri, so how is it that you have become an elephant and are carrying burdens?' He said: 'Your majesty, I did not know its mouth.' Its mouth is fire. Even if a great deal is put into fire, it burns it all. So one who knows this, even if they do much wrong, consumes it all and becomes clean, pure, ageless and immortal.
brihadaranyaka-5-14-8.meaning: Fire is the mouth of the Gayatri; knowing it burns away all wrongdoing.
brihadaranyaka-5-14-8.explanation: A story: a man who claimed to know the Gayatri was reborn as a beast of burden because he missed one key part, its 'mouth', fire. The lesson is that full knowledge purifies, as fire consumes everything put into it.

brihadaranyaka-5-15-1.translation: The face of truth is covered by a golden vessel. Uncover it, O Pushan, so that I who love truth may see. O Pushan, sole seer, Yama, Sun, son of Prajapati, spread out your rays and gather your light. I see your most blessed form. That person yonder, I am he. Let my breath go to the immortal wind, and this body end in ashes. Om. O mind, remember what has been done; remember, O mind, what has been done. O Agni, lead us by the good path to prosperity, O god who knows all our ways. Keep from us crooked wrongdoing. We offer you many words of homage.
brihadaranyaka-5-15-1.meaning: A dying person's prayer to see the truth behind the sun's glare and be led on the good path.
brihadaranyaka-5-15-1.explanation: These verses also appear at the end of the Isha Upanishad. The golden glare of the world hides the truth; the speaker asks the sun to draw back its rays, recognises 'I am that person', and asks fire to guide them after death.

brihadaranyaka-6-1-1.translation: One who knows the eldest and best becomes the eldest and best among their own people. Breath is the eldest and best. One who knows this becomes the eldest and best among their people, and among those they wish to lead.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-1.meaning: Breath is the eldest and best of the body's powers.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-1.explanation: The last chapter opens with the contest of the senses. Breath is named first as the most senior and most important.

brihadaranyaka-6-1-2.translation: One who knows the richest becomes the richest among their own people. Speech is the richest. One who knows this becomes the richest among their people, and among those they wish to lead.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-2.meaning: Speech is the richest power; knowing this brings standing among people.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-2.explanation: Part of a list praising each of the body's powers in turn. Each power brings a matching blessing to the person who understands it.

brihadaranyaka-6-1-3.translation: One who knows the firm base stands firm on level ground and on rough ground. The eye is the firm base, for with the eye one stands firm on level and rough ground. One who knows this stands firm on level and rough ground.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-3.meaning: Sight gives a firm footing in easy and hard places alike.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-3.explanation: The eye lets us see where to step, so it is the 'firm base'. Knowing this gives steadiness in good times and hard ones.

brihadaranyaka-6-1-4.translation: One who knows attainment attains whatever they desire. The ear is attainment, for all the Vedas are attained in the ear. One who knows this attains whatever they desire.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-4.meaning: Hearing is attainment; through it all sacred knowledge is gained.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-4.explanation: The Vedas were learned by listening, so hearing is the power through which knowledge is attained.

brihadaranyaka-6-1-5.translation: One who knows the resting place becomes the resting place of their own people and of others. The mind is the resting place. One who knows this becomes the resting place of their people and of others.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-5.meaning: The mind is the home where everything rests.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-5.explanation: All the senses report to the mind, so it is their resting place. One who knows this becomes a support for others.

brihadaranyaka-6-1-6.translation: One who knows procreation is blessed with offspring and cattle. Semen is procreation. One who knows this is blessed with offspring and cattle.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-6.meaning: The power of procreation brings children and plenty.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-6.explanation: The last power in the list is the generative one, which brings family and wealth.

brihadaranyaka-6-1-7.translation: These powers, arguing about who was best, went to Brahman and asked: 'Who is the richest of us?' He said: 'The one whose departure makes the body seem worst off is the richest among you.'
brihadaranyaka-6-1-7.meaning: The powers ask Brahman which of them is greatest; the test is who the body misses most.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-7.explanation: The famous contest begins. The test is simple: whichever power, when it leaves, makes the body suffer most is the most important.

brihadaranyaka-6-1-8.translation: Speech went out. After staying away for a year it came back and asked: 'How were you able to live without me?' They said: 'Like the dumb who do not speak, but seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, knowing with the mind and procreating with semen, we lived, breathing with breath, and using the other powers.' Speech came back in.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-8.meaning: The body lives on without speech; it is not the most essential power.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-8.explanation: Each sense power leaves for a year to test its importance. The body survives without speech, only unable to speak. This builds toward the lesson that breath is the greatest.

brihadaranyaka-6-1-9.translation: The eye went out. After staying away for a year it came back and asked: 'How were you able to live without me?' They said: 'Like the blind who do not see, but speaking with speech, hearing with the ear, knowing with the mind and procreating with semen, we lived, breathing with breath, and using the other powers.' The eye came back in.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-9.meaning: The body lives on without sight; it is not the most essential power.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-9.explanation: Each sense power leaves for a year to test its importance. The body survives without sight, only unable to see. This builds toward the lesson that breath is the greatest.

brihadaranyaka-6-1-10.translation: The ear went out. After staying away for a year it came back and asked: 'How were you able to live without me?' They said: 'Like the deaf who do not hear, but speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, knowing with the mind and procreating with semen, we lived, breathing with breath, and using the other powers.' The ear came back in.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-10.meaning: The body lives on without hearing; it is not the most essential power.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-10.explanation: Each sense power leaves for a year to test its importance. The body survives without hearing, only unable to hear. This builds toward the lesson that breath is the greatest.

brihadaranyaka-6-1-11.translation: The mind went out. After staying away for a year it came back and asked: 'How were you able to live without me?' They said: 'Like the simple who do not think, but speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear and procreating with semen, we lived, breathing with breath, and using the other powers.' The mind came back in.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-11.meaning: The body lives on without the mind; it is not the most essential power.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-11.explanation: Each sense power leaves for a year to test its importance. The body survives without the mind, only without thought. This builds toward the lesson that breath is the greatest.

brihadaranyaka-6-1-12.translation: Semen went out. After staying away for a year it came back and asked: 'How were you able to live without me?' They said: 'Like the impotent who have no offspring, but speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear and knowing with the mind, we lived, breathing with breath, and using the other powers.' Semen came back in.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-12.meaning: The body lives on without the power of procreation; it is not the most essential power.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-12.explanation: Each sense power leaves for a year to test its importance. The body survives without the power of procreation, only without children. This builds toward the lesson that breath is the greatest.

brihadaranyaka-6-1-13.translation: Then breath, about to leave, tore up the other powers as a great Sindhu horse might tear up the pegs that tether its feet. They said: 'Sir, do not leave! We cannot live without you.' 'Then bring me tribute.' 'So be it.'
brihadaranyaka-6-1-13.meaning: When breath starts to leave, all the other powers are pulled out with it; breath is the greatest.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-13.explanation: The climax of the contest. A powerful horse yanks up its tethering pegs; in the same way, breath's departure would uproot every other power. They all accept breath as their chief.

brihadaranyaka-6-1-14.translation: Speech said: 'The richness that is mine is yours.' The eye: 'The firm base that is mine is yours.' The ear: 'The attainment that is mine is yours.' The mind: 'The resting place that is mine is yours.' Semen: 'The procreation that is mine is yours.' Breath asked: 'Then what is my food, what is my clothing?' 'Whatever there is, down to dogs, worms, insects and moths, is your food; water is your clothing.' For one who knows this as the food of breath, nothing eaten is unfit food and nothing accepted is unfit. So learned priests sip water before and after eating, thinking they thereby clothe breath.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-14.meaning: All the powers give their qualities to breath; all food is breath's food, and water is its clothing.
brihadaranyaka-6-1-14.explanation: Every power admits that its gift really belongs to breath. The custom of sipping water before and after a meal is explained as 'clothing' the breath.

brihadaranyaka-6-2-1.translation: Shvetaketu, son of Aruni, came to the assembly of the Panchalas. He went up to Pravahana Jaivali, who was being attended by his people. Seeing him, the king called out: 'Young man!' He answered: 'Sir!' 'Has your father taught you?' 'Yes,' he said.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-1.meaning: A proud young scholar, Shvetaketu, meets King Pravahana.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-1.explanation: This story, also told in the Chandogya, begins the teaching of the five fires. Shvetaketu thinks his education is complete.

brihadaranyaka-6-2-2.translation: 'Do you know how people go different ways when they depart? How they come back to this world? Why that world is never filled though so many keep going there? After which offering the waters take on a human voice and rise up and speak? Do you know how one reaches the path of the gods or the path of the ancestors? We have heard the seer's words: I have heard of two paths for mortals, of the ancestors and of the gods; by these the whole moving world goes, all that lies between father and mother.' 'I do not know even one of these,' he said.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-2.meaning: The king asks five questions about death and rebirth; Shvetaketu cannot answer any.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-2.explanation: These questions about what happens after death form the framework of the teaching that follows. The young man's ignorance humbles him.

brihadaranyaka-6-2-3.translation: The king invited him to stay, but the boy ignored the invitation and ran off. He went to his father and said: 'So you told me before that I had been fully taught!' 'What is it, wise one?' 'That fellow of the warrior class asked me five questions and I did not know even one.' 'What were they?' He listed their headings.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-3.meaning: Shvetaketu rushes home upset that his father's teaching left gaps.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-3.explanation: He is embarrassed and blames his father. The father calmly asks what the questions were.

brihadaranyaka-6-2-4.translation: His father said: 'My son, you know me: whatever I knew, I told you all of it. But come, let us go there and live as students.' 'You go, sir,' said the boy. So Gautama went to where Pravahana Jaivali was. The king had a seat brought and water fetched for him, and gave him the guest offering. Then he said: 'We grant a boon to the revered Gautama.'
brihadaranyaka-6-2-4.meaning: The humble father goes to the king to learn; the king receives him with honour.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-4.explanation: Gautama (Aruni) admits he does not know and is willing to become a student again. His son is too proud to go. The king welcomes him as an honoured guest.

brihadaranyaka-6-2-5.translation: He said: 'That boon is promised to me. Tell me what you said to the boy.'
brihadaranyaka-6-2-5.meaning: Gautama asks for knowledge, not wealth.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-5.explanation: He chooses the teaching the king mentioned, rather than any material gift.

brihadaranyaka-6-2-6.translation: The king said: 'Gautama, that is among divine boons. Ask for a human one.'
brihadaranyaka-6-2-6.meaning: The king tries to offer worldly gifts instead.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-6.explanation: The king hesitates to share this rare knowledge and suggests wealth.

brihadaranyaka-6-2-7.translation: Gautama said: 'You know I have plenty of gold, cows, horses, servant girls, retinues and clothing. Do not be ungenerous to me with what is great, infinite and boundless.' 'Then, Gautama, you must ask in the proper way.' 'I come to you as a student.' In ancient times people became students just by saying so. So he lived there by declaring himself a student.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-7.meaning: Gautama refuses wealth and formally asks to become the king's student.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-7.explanation: He already has riches; he wants the infinite. By declaring 'I come to you as a student', he accepts the humble place needed to receive the teaching.

brihadaranyaka-6-2-8.translation: The king said: 'Do not hold this against us, Gautama, nor your ancestors. This knowledge has never before lived with any priest. But I will tell it to you, for who could refuse you when you speak like this?'
brihadaranyaka-6-2-8.meaning: The king admits this knowledge was kept among the warrior class, and agrees to share it.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-8.explanation: An unusual moment: a king teaches a priest. The text notes this knowledge had not been held by any Brahmin before.

brihadaranyaka-6-2-9.translation: That world yonder is a fire, Gautama. The sun is its fuel, the rays its smoke, the day its flame, the directions its embers, the in-between directions its sparks. In this fire the gods offer faith. From that offering King Soma arises.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-9.meaning: The first fire is the heavenly world, where faith offered becomes Soma.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-9.explanation: The five-fire teaching sees the cycle of life as a chain of sacrifices. In the first, faith is offered in the sky and becomes Soma, the moon's nectar.

brihadaranyaka-6-2-10.translation: The rain-cloud is a fire, Gautama. The year is its fuel, the clouds its smoke, lightning its flame, thunderbolts its embers, the rumblings its sparks. In this fire the gods offer King Soma. From that offering rain arises.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-10.meaning: The second fire is the rain-cloud, where Soma becomes rain.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-10.explanation: The chain continues: what came from the first fire is offered in the second.

brihadaranyaka-6-2-11.translation: This world is a fire, Gautama. The earth is its fuel, fire its smoke, night its flame, the moon its embers, the stars its sparks. In this fire the gods offer rain. From that offering food arises.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-11.meaning: The third fire is this world, where rain becomes food.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-11.explanation: Rain falling on earth becomes the food that grows from it.

brihadaranyaka-6-2-12.translation: Man is a fire, Gautama. His open mouth is its fuel, breath its smoke, speech its flame, the eye its embers, the ear its sparks. In this fire the gods offer food. From that offering semen arises.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-12.meaning: The fourth fire is the man, where food becomes the seed of life.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-12.explanation: Food eaten by a person is transformed into the power to create new life.

brihadaranyaka-6-2-13.translation: Woman is a fire, Gautama. In this fire the gods offer semen. From that offering a person is born. He lives as long as he lives. Then, when he dies...
brihadaranyaka-6-2-13.meaning: The fifth fire is the woman, where seed becomes a new person.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-13.explanation: The last of the five fires completes the cycle: from faith in heaven to a living human being. The account of what happens after death follows.

brihadaranyaka-6-2-14.translation: ...they carry him to the fire. The fire becomes his fire, the fuel his fuel, the smoke his smoke, the flame his flame, the embers his embers, the sparks his sparks. In this fire the gods offer the person. From that offering the person arises, radiant in colour.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-14.meaning: At death the body is offered to the cremation fire, and the person rises shining.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-14.explanation: Cremation is seen as the final sacrifice. The person offered into the fire emerges in a bright new form, ready for the journey on.

brihadaranyaka-6-2-15.translation: Those who know this, and those who in the forest worship faith as truth, go into the flame, from the flame to the day, from the day to the bright half of the month, from that to the six months when the sun moves north, from those months to the world of the gods, from there to the sun, from the sun to the lightning. A person made of mind comes to those in the lightning and leads them to the worlds of Brahman. They live in those worlds of Brahman for the longest ages. For them there is no return.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-15.meaning: Those who know and live by truth take the path of light to Brahman and do not return.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-15.explanation: This is the 'path of the gods', the way of light. It leads beyond the cycle of birth and death.

brihadaranyaka-6-2-16.translation: Those who win worlds through sacrifice, giving and austerity go into the smoke, from smoke to night, from night to the dark half of the month, from that to the six months when the sun moves south, from those months to the world of the ancestors, and from there to the moon. Reaching the moon they become food, and the gods feed on them there as on King Soma, saying 'grow, wane'. When that is used up, they pass into space, from space to wind, from wind to rain, from rain to earth. Reaching earth they become food. They are offered again in the fire of man, then born in the fire of woman. Rising up to the worlds, they go round in this way. But those who know neither path become worms, insects and biting creatures.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-16.meaning: Those who rely only on good deeds take the path of smoke and return to birth again.
brihadaranyaka-6-2-16.explanation: This is the 'path of the ancestors'. Good deeds bring a stay in a higher world, but when their merit is used up, one returns to be born again. Those who follow neither path fall to the lowest births.

brihadaranyaka-6-3-1.translation: If one wishes 'May I attain greatness', then in the northern course of the sun, in the bright half of the month, on an auspicious day, after a twelve-day vow, one gathers all herbs and fruits in a cup or bowl of fig wood, sweeps and plasters the ground, lays the fire, spreads grass, prepares the butter and, under a male constellation, mixes the mantha drink and offers, saying: 'O Jatavedas, to all the gods in you who turn aside and thwart a person's wishes, I offer their share. May they, pleased, satisfy me with all desires, svāhā. To you who lie across, thinking I am the one who decides all, I offer this stream of butter, you who bring success, svāhā.'
brihadaranyaka-6-3-1.meaning: A rite for someone seeking greatness begins with offerings to win over the powers that block desires.
brihadaranyaka-6-3-1.explanation: Chapter 6.3 describes the 'mantha' rite, a mixed drink of herbs offered with prayers for success. These are ritual instructions, preserved as part of the Upanishad.

brihadaranyaka-6-3-2.translation: Saying 'Svāhā to the eldest, svāhā to the best', one offers into the fire and pours the remainder into the mantha. Likewise with 'Svāhā to breath, svāhā to the richest', 'Svāhā to speech, svāhā to the firm base', 'Svāhā to the eye, svāhā to attainment', 'Svāhā to the ear, svāhā to the resting place', 'Svāhā to the mind, svāhā to procreation', and 'Svāhā to semen'.
brihadaranyaka-6-3-2.meaning: Offerings are made to each life power named in the contest of the senses.
brihadaranyaka-6-3-2.explanation: Each offering honours one of the powers from 6.1, and the drops left on the ladle are poured into the drink, so it gathers their strength.

brihadaranyaka-6-3-3.translation: Saying 'Svāhā to Agni', one offers into the fire and pours the remainder into the mantha. Likewise 'Svāhā to Soma', 'Svāhā to bhūḥ', 'to bhuvaḥ', 'to svaḥ', 'to bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ', 'to the priesthood', 'to the ruling power', 'to the past', 'to the future', 'to the universe', 'to the all', and 'Svāhā to Prajapati'.
brihadaranyaka-6-3-3.meaning: More offerings: to fire, Soma, the three worlds, past, future and the whole.
brihadaranyaka-6-3-3.explanation: The offerings now widen to cover the gods, the worlds and all of time, filling the drink with everything.

brihadaranyaka-6-3-4.translation: Then he touches the drink, saying: 'You are moving. You are glowing. You are full. You are steady. You are the one meeting place. You are the sound hiṅ and what is being sounded. You are the Udgitha and what is being sung. You are what is called out and what is answered. You are blazing in the moist. You are pervading, you are mighty. You are food, you are light. You are the end, you are the gathering-in.'
brihadaranyaka-6-3-4.meaning: The drink is praised as everything, the whole cycle of the chant and of life.
brihadaranyaka-6-3-4.explanation: Touching the drink, the worshipper names it with all the stages of the sacred chant and with the beginning and end of things, treating it as a symbol of breath.

brihadaranyaka-6-3-5.translation: Then he raises it, saying: 'You know all, we know your greatness. He is king, lord and ruler. May he make me king, lord and ruler.'
brihadaranyaka-6-3-5.meaning: Lifting the drink, he prays to gain leadership.
brihadaranyaka-6-3-5.explanation: The drink, standing for breath, is honoured as a king, and the worshipper asks to share its power.

brihadaranyaka-6-3-6.translation: Then he sips it, saying: 'That excellent glory of Savitri. Sweet blow the winds for the righteous, sweet flow the rivers; may the plants be sweet to us. Bhūḥ svāhā. Let us meditate on the light of the god. Sweet be the night and the dawns; sweet the dust of the earth; sweet be heaven our father. Bhuvaḥ svāhā. May he inspire our thoughts. Sweet be the tree to us, sweet the sun; may the cows be sweet to us. Svaḥ svāhā.' He recites the whole Savitri and all the honey verses, saying 'May I become all this. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā.' Finally he sips, washes his hands, and lies down behind the fire with his head to the east. In the morning he worships the sun: 'You are the one lotus of the directions; may I be the one lotus among men.' Returning as he came, he sits behind the fire and recites the lineage.
brihadaranyaka-6-3-6.meaning: He drinks while chanting the Gayatri and the honey verses, asking that all the world be sweet.
brihadaranyaka-6-3-6.explanation: The Gayatri mantra is interwoven, line by line, with the 'madhu' verses wishing sweetness on wind, rivers, plants, day and night. The rite ends with a prayer to the sun at dawn.

brihadaranyaka-6-3-7.translation: Uddalaka Aruni taught this to his pupil Yajnavalkya Vajasaneya and said: 'Even if one were to pour this on a dry stump, branches would grow and leaves would sprout.'
brihadaranyaka-6-3-7.meaning: The rite is so powerful it could make a dead stump grow leaves.
brihadaranyaka-6-3-7.explanation: Part of the chain showing how the mantha rite was handed down, here from Uddalaka Aruni to Yajnavalkya Vajasaneya. The saying about the dry stump praises its life-giving power.

brihadaranyaka-6-3-8.translation: Yajnavalkya Vajasaneya taught this to his pupil Madhuka Paingya and said: 'Even if one were to pour this on a dry stump, branches would grow and leaves would sprout.'
brihadaranyaka-6-3-8.meaning: The rite is so powerful it could make a dead stump grow leaves.
brihadaranyaka-6-3-8.explanation: Part of the chain showing how the mantha rite was handed down, here from Yajnavalkya Vajasaneya to Madhuka Paingya. The saying about the dry stump praises its life-giving power.

brihadaranyaka-6-3-9.translation: Madhuka Paingya taught this to his pupil Chula Bhagavitti and said: 'Even if one were to pour this on a dry stump, branches would grow and leaves would sprout.'
brihadaranyaka-6-3-9.meaning: The rite is so powerful it could make a dead stump grow leaves.
brihadaranyaka-6-3-9.explanation: Part of the chain showing how the mantha rite was handed down, here from Madhuka Paingya to Chula Bhagavitti. The saying about the dry stump praises its life-giving power.

brihadaranyaka-6-3-10.translation: Chula Bhagavitti taught this to his pupil Janaki Ayasthuna and said: 'Even if one were to pour this on a dry stump, branches would grow and leaves would sprout.'
brihadaranyaka-6-3-10.meaning: The rite is so powerful it could make a dead stump grow leaves.
brihadaranyaka-6-3-10.explanation: Part of the chain showing how the mantha rite was handed down, here from Chula Bhagavitti to Janaki Ayasthuna. The saying about the dry stump praises its life-giving power.

brihadaranyaka-6-3-11.translation: Janaki Ayasthuna taught this to his pupil Satyakama Jabala and said: 'Even if one were to pour this on a dry stump, branches would grow and leaves would sprout.'
brihadaranyaka-6-3-11.meaning: The rite is so powerful it could make a dead stump grow leaves.
brihadaranyaka-6-3-11.explanation: Part of the chain showing how the mantha rite was handed down, here from Janaki Ayasthuna to Satyakama Jabala. The saying about the dry stump praises its life-giving power.

brihadaranyaka-6-3-12.translation: Satyakama Jabala taught this to his pupils and said: 'Even if one were to pour this on a dry stump, branches would grow and leaves would sprout.' One should not teach it to anyone who is not one's son or pupil.
brihadaranyaka-6-3-12.meaning: The rite is passed on, and should be taught only to one's son or student.
brihadaranyaka-6-3-12.explanation: The chain of transmission ends with a rule of secrecy: this knowledge is shared only within close teaching bonds.

brihadaranyaka-6-3-13.translation: Four things are of fig wood: the ladle, the cup, the fuel and the two stirring sticks. There are ten kinds of village grain: rice and barley, sesame and beans, millet and panic seed, wheat, lentils, pulses and vetch. These are ground and soaked in curd, honey and butter, and an offering of butter is made.
brihadaranyaka-6-3-13.meaning: The rite uses fig-wood tools and ten kinds of grain mixed with curd, honey and butter.
brihadaranyaka-6-3-13.explanation: Practical details of the mantha rite: what the utensils are made of and what goes into the drink.
